#2853. Fantasy Football Rankings: Hayden Winks' RB Blueprint for Week 9

The Blueprint is my weekly column and basically everything that I use to build out the most accurate rankings I can. There will be this RB column, a WR column and a combination column on the onesie positions. You will find film notes and endless charts. Maybe enough charts to stress test the Yahoo website. I kid.

It's impossible to get every ranking thoroughly early in the week, so be sure to keep checking in on these columns through Sunday morning. As always, my full rankings at every position are available.

1. Jahmyr Gibbs (at MIA) - 133.5 proj. total yards

Gibbs survived the Vikings matchup with a top-5 finish in Week 8. Things will get easier from there. A lot easier. Across the season, Gibbs is averaging 25.5 half PPR points (RB1) on 23.7 expected points (RB1). He's leading in carries per game and second in receptions per game. What a season.

Miami ranks ninth-worst in half PPR points allowed to opposing backfields (22.5 per game) and sits second in receiving points allowed to RBs. Detroit carries an implied team total of 28.75 points (third) as 7-point road favorites. This is obviously a smash spot, duh.

2. Kenneth Walker III (vs. NYJ) - 113.5 proj. total yards

Walker has had slower games against the Seahawks and healthy Broncos defenses, both clearly top-5 units to me right now. It hasn't helped that LT Josh Simmons (back/other) and LG Kingsley Suamataia (benched) haven't been active, forcing the Chiefs to dial up a ton of their runs to the right side only. Still, Walker is the RB6 on RB3 usage this month and RB2 in both metrics across the entire season. The offense at least getting Rashee Rice back in the mix will help them move the ball more often.

The Jets placed star DT T'Vondre Sweat on IR and first-round rookie DE David Bailey has missed time recently, too. They bottled up Mike Washington Jr. and the Raiders' disaster-class OL last week, but they're a unit to attack right now. Kansas City carries an implied total of 28 points (fourth) as 9.5-point home favorites.

3. Christian McCaffrey (vs. LV) - 107.5 proj. total yards

Update: Mike Evans (Achilles) and Deebo Samuel Sr. (hamstring) aren't available. Neither is Brandon Aiyuk if you were wondering.

McCaffrey is the RB6 in half PPR points per game on RB6 usage across his last four games. They needed more receiving work from CMC during this stretch with Deebo Samuel Sr. and Mike Evans missing time, and we'll see if they return off the bye. He's better without them but has been a mid-range RB1 with the WRs healthy.

The Raiders rank fifth in half PPR points allowed to opposing backfields (23.4 per game) and sit third in rushing points allowed to RBs, recently surrendering an RB6 finish to Braelon Allen. San Francisco enters with a slate-high 30.5-point implied team total (first) as 9.5-point home favorites. It's a great spot.

4. Bijan Robinson (vs. CIN) - 122.5 proj. total yards

Update: Brian Robinson Jr. (hamstring) went to IR, and they called up Khalil Herbert.

Robinson is the RB30 on RB23 usage this month. I can promise that'll be the worst stretch of his season.

The primary driver of the falloff is the on/off splits with Michael Penix Jr. as a receiver. His targets with Penix this year are 3.2 per game. His career average for context is 5.1. Part of this is Penix's inability to move, which is required to buy time in the screen game or to work to the checkdown. The ball is flying out of his hand early in the snap, and those are less likely to go to RBs. Hopefully they carve out more looks moving forward. It'd be enough of a difference to view him in the mid-range RB1 tier, instead of the elite RB1 tier.

The Bengals are much improved against the run with superstar DT Dexter Lawrence shutting down everything up the middle, but the rest of the defense is looking suspect, especially if CB1 DJ Turner (ankle) can't go. The LB and S groups are missing huge tackles weekly, and Robinson is a great candidate to rip wide zone explosives away from Lawrence in the A gap. This is what Tony Pollard did last week when he was the RB3 overall. The Falcons carry a 24.25-point implied team total (12th) as 3-point home underdogs.

5. D'Andre Swift (vs. TB) - 88.5 proj. total yards

Update: Kyle Monangai (turf toe) is unlikely to play. The splits with Kyle Monangai are staggering. We'll see if he can get cleared this week. If not, Swift has enjoyed a month-long stretch of being the RB3 on RB2 usage overall.

Tampa Bay has once again been stout against backfields this season, ranking 31st in half PPR points allowed to RBs (14.5 per game). The Buccaneers have been especially tough on the ground, sitting 31st in rushing points allowed per game to the position. Just ask Bijan Robinson (RB28), Jaylen Warren (RB23) and Javonte Williams (RB19) this month. Chicago enters as 5.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 26.5 points (seventh).

6. Javonte Williams (at IND) - 83.5 proj. total yards

Williams' lack of explosives is starting to cause the Cowboys' games, like last week in the second half when they leaned on the run game and it went nowhere. For fantasy purposes, it largely hasn't mattered because of his red-zone role in this top-10 offense. He's the RB12 on RB4 usage this season, despite being the RB11 in carries and RB23 in receptions.

His fantasy RB1 value is completely tied to scoring touchdowns. Since joining the Cowboys, he's averaged 16.5 points when they've scored 30+ points versus 15.1 in the 20s and 9.4 in the teens.

The good news is the Cowboys project for 28.75 points (second) against a Colts defense that looks lifeless without DT DeForest Buckner. Bhayshul Tuten just finished as the RB2 without playing the fourth quarter, and Chris Rodriguez Jr. was trucking defenders himself. Indianapolis has allowed the sixth-most rushing yards per game this season, and that will probably only get worse.

7. Rhamondre Stevenson (vs. GB) - 86.5 proj. total yards

Update: TreVeyon Henderson (illness) was ruled out again. I hope he is alright. There is a history brewing here, and he's so young. Here's more on that:

There are notable splits for Stevenson whether he plays or not. In seven games dating back to last year where Hendo missed or had fewer than five carries, Stevenson is the RB13 on RB16 usage. He drops to RB25 on RB39 usage in the other 19 games. This year, Stevenson is the RB20 on RB28 usage while he's been in and out of the mix. It helps if A.J. Brown and Hunter Henry join Romeo Doubs and Mack Hollins on the sideline, too.

Green Bay represents a favorable rushing matchup, ranking seventh in half PPR points allowed to RBs at 23.1 per game. The Packers sit sixth in points allowed to RB rushing at 16.6 per game, having yielded top-24 fantasy finishes to Chuba Hubbard (RB7), Jahmyr Gibbs (RB18), Javonte Williams (RB17) and D'Andre Swift (RB12) in four consecutive weeks. New England hosts the Packers as 3-point home favorites with an implied team total of 25.25 points (10th).

8. James Cook III (at MIN) - 97.5 proj. total yards

Truly nothing has changed. Cook is the RB4 on RB9 usage this season, averaging 101 rushing YPG (third) on RB41 receptions per game. The Bills offense looked particularly great last week with DJ Moore stretching the field and Dalton Kincaid ripping explosives in multiple TE sets.

The challenge here is the Vikings defense. They just held the Lions to 19 points on the road and are clearly one of the only truly elite defenses. Detroit leaned on the ground game a bit more than usual against them, a trend that's appeared throughout the season against Minnesota. It's allowed the No. 16 rushing YPG versus the No. 31 passing YPG. Opposing offenses have a 45% neutral pass rate against them (second lowest). That said, Jahmyr Gibbs (RB5) and Jonathan Taylor (RB8) both held the line, while mediocre schemes/players have completely busted. Buffalo heads to Minnesota as 3.5-point road favorites with a 25-point implied team total (11th).

9. Bucky Irving (at CHI) - 83.5 proj. total yards

The Bucs are coming off the craziest two-game run script I can remember. Irving has been the RB4 and RB11, respectively in expected half PPR points in them, while Kenny Gainwell has popped off alongside him. Tampa Bay is content running the ball behind its fantastic OL, and while it won't be anywhere near this extreme, I don't see that game plan changing after Baker Mayfield struggled in a pass-first offense early on. Irving's vision and contact balance are a great fit to consistently hit these 20-yard runs. This month, Irving is the RB2 on RB3 usage. He handled the goal-line carry last week, while Sean Tucker looked on from the sideline.

The Bears defense has been stingy against opposing backfields, ranking 29th in half PPR points allowed to running backs at 16.7 per game. Then they added the best DT in Jeffery Simmons. This will be a tough test for an on-fire Bucs run game. The Bears held Bijan Robinson to an RB31 finish in Week 6 and bottled up both Seahawks RBs last week. Tampa Bay heads on the road as 5.5-point road underdogs with an implied team total of 21 points (22nd).

10. Jonathan Taylor (vs. DAL) - 85.5 proj. total yards

Taylor had his worst game since Week 8 of 2024. That did come against the best fantasy RB defense (Jaguars), but it did also come without LG Quenton Nelson during the middle of Taylor's own trade talks. The Colts been mixing in Seth McGowen earlier in games more than they did before, and their defense is getting blown out, which means Taylor can get scripted out of games. It's nowhere near the same situation as before, dropping him to boom-bust RB2 levels. I anticipate him being far more matchup-elastic given his poor surroundings.

Luckily, the Cowboys are a great spot. They've allowed the third-most fantasy points to RBs on the most rushing yards per game (152.8). It was Tyler Allgeier's turn last week (RB1 overall), but Saquon Barkley looked good on his limited touches the week prior and Bucky Irving dropped 175 yards in Week 5, too. It's bad versus bad on this side of the ball. The Colts have a 22.75-point team total here. It's a much better spot than last week, pending reports that Taylor's role could be changed the week before the trade deadline.

11. Kyren Williams (at WAS) - 86.5 proj. total yards

Williams' role is nearly the same, but the Rams offense hasn't been quite as explosive recently, so his output has slightly turned down. This month, he's the RB17 on RB16 usage, averaging 14.5 carries and 3.0 receptions. He was catching more passes early on, and it's possible the increased usage of 13-personnel is working against his passing role. Blake Corum continues to play every other drive; Corum is an NFL starter on tape to me.

Washington sits 27th in half PPR points allowed to opposing backfields at 17.0 per game on the season, but DT Daron Payne just went to IR. The top-end RBs have played well, including Christian McCaffrey (RB2) and Jonathan Taylor (RB9). Even Saquon Barkley (RB21 in a part-time role) looked good last week. The Rams travel as 5.5-point road favorites, carrying an implied team total of 26.5 points (eighth).

12. Chuba Hubbard (vs. DEN) - 90.5 proj. total yards

Update: Star LG Damien Lewis (knee) is out. It's a bad game to miss with menace DT Zach Allen on deck.

Hubbard has been a high-volume anchor, sitting as the RB9 in per-game half PPR points on RB6 usage across his last four contests despite some difficult matchups. He's handled 19.3 carries per game (RB7) over that window, crossing the 20-carry threshold in three of those four outings. In Week 8 against Green Bay, Hubbard set season highs with eight targets and seven receptions, turning that receiving work into 21.4 half PPR points on 24.1 expected points. Jonathon Brooks is starting to practice, but they'll ramp him up slowly and he's unlikely to factor in too much when he is cleared.

The Broncos defense ranks 11th in half PPR points allowed to RBs at 21.9 per game on the season, but their starting lineup is finally back to normal. Opponents have had success through the air against Denver, where the defense allows 8.5 half PPR points per game to receiving RBs (fourth-most in the NFL), highlighted by Emmett Johnson's RB5 finish in Week 8. Carolina's offense also brings distinctive passing tendencies, holding a 62% neutral pass rate that ranks third-highest in the league. The Panthers enter the matchup as 3-point home underdogs with an implied team total of 20.25 points (25th).

13. Josh Jacobs (at NE) - 69.5 proj. total yards

Jacobs was the RB1 overall in usage last week after being the RB5 in expected half PPR points in his debut. He's averaging 18.9 half PPR points on 23.4 expected, essentially trading a couple of runs for a couple of targets in this more pass-heavy Packers offense. That's a great trade-off in fantasy. For context, the Packers had a 46% neutral pass rate in 2024-25 versus a 56% rate this year.

On tape, Jacobs is not in his prime, nor is the Packers offensive line, so he'll definitely be an inefficient player. Green Bay can't trust MarShawn Lloyd in protection or to hit the right hole, so they'll live with whatever Jacobs can produce.

The Patriots rank 26th in half PPR points allowed to opposing running backs, giving up just 17.0 points per game to the position. This was true the year prior, so it's a matchup worth knocking expectations. Recent bell cows D'Andre Swift (RB13) and Braelon Allen (RB19) were just fine. Green Bay heads on the road as 3-point road underdogs with an implied team total of 22.25 points (17th).

14. Chase Brown (at ATL) - 75.5 proj. total yards

Brown was the RB20 on RB14 usage last week despite finishing with eight receptions. The good news is Brown still has 8-catch grabs in his pocket and those eventually will lead to more explosives and touchdowns. The problem was he played 2 of 8 snaps inside the 10-yard line, including 1 of 4 inside the 5-yard line. That's where Samaje Perine is mixing in more than normal. Across the month, Brown is the dang RB39 on RB11 usage. He'll settle in as a fantasy RB2 with upside, but the pass game is too good and Brown is too mid to believe in a full top-10 RB1 rebound here.

The matchup with the Falcons is a solid one. They've allowed the sixth-most points to fantasy RBs and were just embarrassed by Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell last week. Atlanta has allowed a top-10 fantasy RB in 4 straight outings, and EDGE Samson Ebukam just went to IR. They've missed a LB, too. The Bengals project for 27.75 points (fifth).

Tuten is a game-time decision with an ankle/foot injury. He hasn't practiced yet but his last play in Week 8 was a touchdown that didn't look painful. This is a good reminder that Chris Rodriguez Jr. is one of the top insurance options in fantasy.

Tuten sits as the RB10 in per-game half PPR scoring on RB18 usage over his last four contests. He has generated efficient production on the ground and through the air, averaging 72 rushing yards (RB13) and 36.3 receiving yards per game (RB7) across that window. Coming off a bye in Week 8, Tuten set season highs with 28.9 half PPR points (RB2) and 104 rushing yards against Indianapolis. The potential for a low-end RB1 finish following that Week 7 bye is pretty clear.

The Ravens present a difficult matchup, ranking 23rd in half PPR points allowed to running backs at 17.3 per game. Baltimore is particularly stout against pass-catching backs, ranking 29th by allowing just 3.7 half PPR receiving points per game. That matches its recent stretch, having limited Chase Brown (RB36) and Bijan Robinson (RB18) to modest days in Weeks 7 and 5, respectively. The Jaguars enter Thursday night as 8.5-point road favorites with an implied total of 25.5 points (ninth).

16. Woody Marks (at LAC) - 78.5 proj. total yards

It sounds like David Montgomery is going to miss another one. In three games without him, Marks is the RB29 on RB17 usage, 16.3 carries and 2.7 targets per game. Marks is a replacement-level back who can play in all phases, but expecting efficient outings behind this OL is asking too much. He's finished below his expected half PPR point totals in 5 of 7 games.

The good news is the Chargers' run defense isn't one to fear. They rank 10th in half PPR points allowed to opposing backfields at 22.2 per game. Los Angeles has been particularly vulnerable against ground games, ranking fourth in rushing points allowed per game to running backs (17.3) while ranking 27th against RB receiving. It's allowed a top-16 finish in 4 straight games, including Blake Corum (RB15), Kenneth Walker (RB1), J.K. Dobbins (RB16), and Emanuel Wilson (RB6). Houston enters the contest as 4.5-point road favorites with a 22.5-point implied team total (16th).

17. Jonah Coleman (at CAR) - 83.5 proj. total yards

With RJ Harvey (knee) on IR, the backfield was down to two. JK Dobbins started, but just like last week, it was Coleman who ended it. Dobbins was held to just one (one) snap in the second half of Week 8, while Coleman was left wide open for a 51-yard reception and ultimately cut back on a separate carry for a score. He finished as the RB11 on RB6 usage, tallying 11 carries and four receptions. He handled goal-line carries on separate drives, too.

Coleman has a little windup step when buying time as a runner, and he can find some cutback lanes that others won't see. He is a low-built power runner who will try to lower his shoulder for an extra yard. At the same time, he's probably the slowest fantasy starter and did bounce some runs to play into his weakness. He looks like a Day 3 talent who is climbing the depth chart by having fresh legs with some established trust. It's unlikely that Dobbins ever threatens on passing downs, so Coleman is at least the passing-down back with an emerging rushing role. We'll see if the Broncos actually trade for Jonathan Taylor later on. For now, Coleman is an RB2/3.

The upcoming matchup brings a Carolina defense allowing 26.1 half PPR points per game to running backs (second most). The Panthers have been particularly vulnerable on the ground, ranking second in rushing fantasy points allowed to opposing backfields. Recent opposing rushers have capitalized, including Bucky Irving (RB2) and Josh Jacobs (RB10). Denver heads in as 3-point road favorites with an implied team total of 23.25 points (13th).

18. Ollie Gordon II (vs. DET) - 78.5 proj. total yards

Gordon has taken on significant rushing volume, ranking as the RB16 in half PPR points per game on RB12 usage across his last four outings. Over that stretch, he is averaging 17.8 carries (10th) and 90 rushing yards (eighth), while logging nine carries inside the 5-yard line. His passing-game involvement remains minimal, however, so the risk of being scripted out of the game plan is concerning against great opponents.

The matchup is tough against a Lions defense allowing just 16.2 half PPR points per game to RBs (30th most). Detroit ranks 25th in rushing points allowed and 24th in receiving points allowed to opposing backfields. Miami operates with a run-heavy approach, ranking 30th in neutral pass rate at 44%, while Detroit opponents pass at an extreme 59% clip (third highest). The Dolphins enter as 7-point home underdogs with an implied total of 21.75 points (18th).

Lions LB Jack Campbell will not be out there. It was relieving to hear that he has movement in his lower extremities.

19. Devin Singletary (at PHI) - 75.5 proj. total yards

Update: Cam Skattebo (hamstring) is doubtful. Tyrone Tracy Jr. (hamstring) is on IR. Najee Harris isn't coming back. It's Singletary and backup RBs I've never heard of. He's been with the team for awhile and is fairly trusted, even if he doesn't offer much beyond what is in front of him. That's okay in fantasy football. We're here for the touches. For reference, the Giants' RB room has averaged 19.5 expected half PPR points, and Singletary is probably looking at 75% of that here. We're approaching "Too Big To Fail" territory.

The Eagles' run defense hasn't lived up to their potential. Their DTs are hot and cold in a lost season, and their EDGEs aren't as good as they've been in previous DC Vic Fangio defenses. The Giants have a solid 20.75-point team total (21st) despite being on the road. They are field goal favorites, though Singletary is pretty game script proof.

20. Derrick Henry (vs. JAX) - 80.5 proj. total yards

Henry has played seven games without Lamar Jackson over the last three years, and he's averaging 16.8 half PPR points on 17.5 expected points and 22 carries per game. That's the absolute upside case, but the reality is his new baseline is far lower with Tyler Huntley also out and with OC Declan Doyle finding more ways to move the ball than running behind an aging Henry. The last month of the year are a great example of that, when he's been the RB28 on RB17 usage and 17.3 carries per game. That's a better baseline with "Joe Fagnano" under center on Thursday Night Football.

Jacksonville has been the most difficult fantasy RB matchup this year, allowing just 14.2 half PPR points per game to the position on the fewest rushing YPG (77.4). Opposing offenses have the lowest neutral run rate against them, too. It'll be a little easier without DT DaVon Hamilton, but this remains a matchup to avoid. The Ravens only have a 14.75-point team total as 10-point dogs. Henry can get game-scripted out of outings, just as Jonathan Taylor (RB37 on RB20) usage was last week.

21. Ashton Jeanty (at SF) - 64.5 proj. total yards

Jeanty is the first player to have the same or fewer carries in 8 straight games to open a season, per Doug Clawson on X. I don't think this was pre-game comments or ankle-related either. Coach Klint Kubiak has been scaling down his carries for a long time and communicated to Jeanty before this game of the role change.

Week 8 easily could be a one-game experiment to fix a completely broken run game, but it'd be a surprise if Jeanty went back to his early-season workhorse role. It's clear Kubiak, who pounded the table for Mike Washington Jr. and wasn't around for the Jeanty top-10 selection, views this duo as closer to even than Twitter does. Some of that is scheme-related, as Washington is a better athlete for the wide zone, while Jeanty's power-based skill set is struggling to find cutback lanes and hit the hole in time.

Jeanty's pass-game role is very safe, and I'm currently projecting a more even split on early-down runs, just how it has been from Week 3 on when he's been the RB18 on RB15 usage. The error bars here are obviously extremely wide, but if there's a game script that leans Jeanty, it's clearly while trailing. The Raiders are 10-point dogs to the 49ers.

22. Quinshon Judkins (at NO) - 81.5 proj. total yards

Judkins' role is changing for the worse with Dylan Sampson back in the mix. His expected half PPR points have dropped from 13.8 to 11.4 since his return and all of that has come from the receiving game, where his targets' split is 4.0 to 1.5. If the Browns start trailing, Judkins is now at risk of a total dud. He's been the RB22 and RB26 in usage over the last two outings and has been fairly inefficient throughout the year, making him a FLEX rather than a fantasy RB2.

The Saints represent a prime rushing matchup, ranking first in half PPR points allowed to running backs at 27.9 per game. New Orleans has been especially vulnerable on the ground, allowing a league-high 21.2 points per game to RB rushing (first of 32). Over their last four games, the Saints have yielded spike performances to Bijan Robinson (RB5), Brian Robinson (RB8), Aaron Jones (RB7) and Tyrone Tracy (RB8). Cleveland travels as 2.5-point road underdogs with an implied total of 20.5 points (24th).

23. Saquon Barkley (vs. NYG) - 68.5 proj. total yards

Update: Barkley was only able to muster up a limited practice this week in practice, a sign that his lingering injuries haven't fully healed.

Barkley scored in the red zone on a Wildcat run, showcasing enough speed to get to the pylon. He generally looked just fine on tape, but the Eagles had to bring down his workload again. He's been the RB32 and RB22 in usage over the past two games, and in Week 8, he played just one snap on late downs and 44% of snaps on early downs. It'll be hard to reach top-15 status until he's unbothered by his back and hamstring.

A date with the Giants is neutral, revenge game aside. They're mediocre against the run in general, but both teams can play a run-heavy, slow-paced style that limits fantasy points in general. The Eagles only have an 18.0-point team total; we'll see if anything changes with QB Joe Milton starting over Tanner McKee.

24. Alvin Kamara (vs. CLE) - 63.5 proj. total yards

Update: Travis Etienne (hamstring) is due back in the next two weeks but not yet. The Saints fired their OL coach during the bye week, then released Kendre Miller on Saturday. On top of that, CJ Donaldson (shoulder) was ruled out. Miller and Donaldson have taken a third of the workload each without Etienne. He'll compete with Audric Estime this week, and Estime is really limited to downhill rushing. It's the best Kamara has looked all year. He's been the RB24 on RB43 usage this past month and was up to RB23 usage in Week 7. He's a great FLEX play.

Cleveland ranks 17th in half PPR points allowed per game to opposing running backs (19.3). The Browns have been far more vulnerable to ground attacks than pass-catching backs, ranking 9th in rushing points allowed per game to backfields but 30th against RB receiving (3.5 points per game). Cleveland has given up big games on the ground over recent weeks, including 143 rushing yards and an RB9 finish to Jaylen Warren in Week 8 and an RB1 overall finish to Tony Pollard in Week 7. New Orleans is listed as 2.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 23.0 points (14th).

25. Jadarian Price (vs. ARI) - 69.5 proj. total yards

The backfield is set. Emanuel Wilson was active but didn't play and is on track to be a healthy scratch moving forward, leaving Zach Charbonnet, Jadarian Price and George Holani as the active players. Charbonnet started and played 37% of snaps, leading to 11.6 expected half PPR points (RB22 usage). Price played 48% of snaps, leading to 9.9 expected half PPR points (RB30). Holani played 17%. The trio played on both early and late downs, pass-protected, ran routes and carried the ball.

It's officially a "let-the-best-man-win" committee, for an organization that held back Kenneth Walker III for years. So who looked the best? Take a look at this:

Athletically, it's no contest. Price is so much faster in a straight line and laterally agile. The speed difference is evident on the outside runs, while the lateral ability is easier to see on the cutback runs. That's not the end-all, be all, but it absolutely does matter and it's unlikely to change with Charbonnet coming off a February ACL surgery. Price was the one to receive the pitch on a sweep, so the coaching staff obviously agrees.

That said, Price did have two reps where he probably could've done a lot more with the look. One of them featured him not giving his center the time to climb to the next level. He instead jammed into a crowded lane, where a more patient and crafty runner would've cut back for a nice gain. The other rep was attempting to bounce it outside of nickel CB Kyler Gordon, when he could've hit his inside shoulder hard for a potential nice gain. Neither was egregious, but the top-end veterans treat them differently.

Charbonnet's runs were more textbook, but there was space to carve out real explosives if he was simply faster. Both of the runs in the video above showcase that glaring flaw. I'd understand they always value Charbonnet's size and quality decision-making in short yardage, but the Seahawks would do well if they continued giving Price a lot of the early-down and between-the-20s runs to increase their odds of an explosive and to give Price more time on task to develop.

Arizona ranks 18th in half PPR points allowed to opposing running backs, yielding 19.3 fantasy points per game to the position. The Cardinals sit 19th against RB rushing and 18th against RB receiving, having recently surrendered big finishes like Jahmyr Gibbs (RB1) in Week 5. Seattle enters as 11.5-point home favorites with a 28-point team total (fifth). They didn't have DT Walter Nolen last week and EDGE Josh Sweat is on the trade block.

26. Blake Corum (at WAS) - 59.5 proj. total yards

Corum is very good, as is the rushing scheme and blocking. It's also helping that Matthew Stafford's elbow is bothering him, which has led the offense into very long drives. Corum can't keep up this RB12 on RB40 usage pace from the past month, but he has been the RB26 on average this season. He's getting every other drive and projects better in positive game scripts. The Rams are 4.5-point road favorites here with the No. 7 team total (26.0).

27. Rachaad White (vs. LAR) - 57.5 proj. total yards

Jeremy McNichols (foot) is going to miss months, leaving White and Austin Ekeler at the top of the pecking order with Devin Neal and Craig Reynolds available from the practice squad. White and Ekeler are battling it out in all phases, with White starting last week and finishing off the win with an explosive and goal-line TD late in the fourth quarter. White was the RB17 on RB17 usage last week and was the RB11 on RB22 usage before that. His fantasy low-end RB2 case is pretty straightforward.

The Rams rank 27th in half PPR points allowed per game to opposing backfields (17.0). Their DL is strong enough to overcome a scheme that is daring teams to run. Offenses facing Los Angeles have posted a 47% neutral pass rate, which is the third-lowest rate in the league. Because the Rams are light in the box and teams are often trailing, they have allowed the seventh-most receiving points to RBs, which plays into White's game. Ashton Jeanty was a PPR scam in Week 7 (RB10), and Bam Knight (RB20) and James Cook III (RB4) got home in the weeks before that. Washington is listed as a 5.5-point home underdog with an implied team total of 21.0 points (23rd).

28. Breece Hall (at KC) - 66.5 proj. total yards

Update: Hall was able to rack up back-to-back full practices this week and will play. We'll see how the split looks, but Hall is unlikely to return to his RB12, RB13 and RB33 finishes to start the year with Braelon Allen playing so well in his absence. That's particularly true with the Chiefs on deck. They've allowed the 25th-most rushing yards per game (96.3). If forced to guess, Hall starts the game and is the primary pass-catching back, while Allen mixes in fairly even in terms of carries. It's possible Allen even steals goal-line looks after plenty of between-tackles success so far. A two-back committee with a 19.5-point team total is that of a zero-floor FLEX. It doesn't help that the Jets have been linked in trade talks with Hall.

29. Tyler Allgeier (at SEA) - 70.5 proj. total yards

With Jeremiyah Love (ankle) picking up his third separate high ankle sprain of the season, Allgeier has a chance to consolidate most of the Cardinals' touches. We'll see if Bam Knight (concussion) can get cleared in time. Without him, Allgeier is looking like one of the biggest workhorses of the week. The Cardinals' RB room collectively has averaged 21.5 expected half PPR points per game this year, and if he inherits 80% of that, then he's a top-24 option.

That will be stress-tested against the Seahawks, however. Gardner Minshew will make his first start against a top-2 defense. They've only allowed 94.0 YPG on the ground this year, and they recently kept Kenneth Walker III to 57 and Christian McCaffrey to 83 total yards. D'Andre Swift's 3-score outing on Monday Night Football is absolutely the exception, and the Cardinals unit is nowhere near the Bears'. Arizona has a highly concerning 14.5-point team total.

31. Zach Charbonnet (vs. ARI) - 56.5 proj. total yards

32. Jordan Mason (vs. BUF) - 52.5 proj. total yards

33. Aaron Jones Sr. (vs. BUF) - 44.5 proj. total yards

The Vikings backfield is so split down the middle that it's rendering both backs next to useless, at least until they figure out how to score more points. Minnesota is 31st in RB usage this season, averaging just 17.4 expected half PPR points to the entire backfield. If this hovers around a 50/50 split, then Jones and Jordan Mason are in the 7-10 points range on average. Last week, it was even worse because game script went away from them. Jones was the RB43 in usage (5.3 expected points), while Mason was the RB47.

Game script isn't expected to be better this week against the Bills. The Vikings are 3-point dogs with a team total of 20.75 points (23rd). The Bills have been pretty bad against fantasy RBs this season, but these teams also haven't had Carson Wentz at QB. To Jones' credit, the Bills rank 11th against RB rushing (14.1 points allowed per game) and 3rd against RB receiving (9.3 points allowed per game). Jones is more likely to catch passes, while Mason is more live for a goal-line plunge.

With Breece Hall (quad) practicing in full and calling himself "the starter", it's officially time to scale back Allen's role. In the 3 games with him to start the year, Allen was nowhere near fantasy viable, seeing just 8 total opportunities per game.

Now, he's earned more work than that, but it'll be surprising if he catches many passes at all or clears more than 12 carries. The Jets have averaged 18.4 expected half PPR points (28th) to their RB room across the entire season, and Allen should be somewhere in the 30-50% range of it moving forward. 40% of that means 7.4 expected points, essentially a pretty tough FLEX to fantasy RB4. There's more upside with him because he may be their goal line back, but Allen is best viewed as a Brian Robinson Jr. type.

This matchup is scary as well. The Chiefs are 25th in rushing yards allowed, and New York is expected to lose by 9.5 points. That game script works in Hall's favor. Not Allen's.

35. Mike Washington Jr. (at SF) - 40.5 proj. total yards

As President of the "Mike Washington might eat into Ashton Jeanty's workload" Club, this is not the week to double down on what happened last week when Klint Kubiak experimented with very clear roles. Washington was fine behind a terrible Raiders' OL on tape, but he didn't do anything extra either. Jeanty will handle all pass down work and may even sub in at the goal line as the more powerful short-yardage back, so even if Washington is a between-the-20s ballcarrier, we have to be careful with matchups. The Raiders are 8.5-point dogs to the 49ers, who might have Nick Bosa back.

37. Omarion Hampton (vs. HOU) - 28.5 proj. total yards

41. Kenneth Gainwell (at CHI) - 34.5 proj. total yards

42. J.K. Dobbins (at CAR) - 38.5 proj. total yards

43. Samaje Perine (at ATL) - 26.5 proj. total yards

44. Roschon Johnson (at TB) - 24.5 proj. total yards

45. Emmett Johnson (vs. NYJ) - 30.5 proj. total yards

Johnson is so much more valuable than the TE2, WR5 and QB2 currently on your bench.

#2851. Hardik Pandya-Arshdeep Singh trade: What do MI and PBKS stand to gain from the deal

Hardik Pandya-Arshdeep Singh trade: What do MI and PBKS stand to gain from the deal originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Hardik Pandya is set to join Punjab Kings in exchange for Arshdeep Singh, with the trade reportedly completed.

Mumbai Indians, who finished ninth in IPL 2026 with four wins from 14 matches, gain a left-arm new-ball and death-overs specialist to pair with Jasprit Bumrah.

Punjab Kings gain a fast-bowling all-rounder under Shreyas Iyer but take on Hardik's injury risk and lose their all-time leading wicket-taker.

After months of trade rumours and uncertainties, Hardik Pandya's home ahead of the 2027 IPL might be decided in the most shocking way possible. According to multiple reports, the Mumbai Indians and the Punjab Kings have agreed on one of the biggest trades in IPL history, with Hardik Pandya moving to Punjab and Arshdeep Singh going the other way ahead of IPL 2027.

An IPL source has confirmed that the trade has been completed and that Hardik is pleased to play under Shreyas Iyer, who continues as Punjab's captain. Hardik's three-year stint as Mumbai captain has been disappointing, with the franchise making the playoffs just once and losing 24 of their 39 matches.

In contrast, Arshdeep has been in excellent form in recent seasons, even helping Punjab reach the finals against RCB last year. His 111 wickets in 96 matches at an economy rate of 9.18 has also been a big part of his appeal.

Both teams have until the retention deadline on November 17, and the mini-auction takes place in Goa on December 16. Here is what each side stands to gain.

MORE: 'GG never accepted mediocrity' - Iyer reveals Gambhir's high standards with KKR

The clearest gain is bowling support for Bumrah. No Mumbai bowler took more than 15 wickets in IPL 2026, with Allah Ghazanfar leading the list with 15. Arshdeep took 14 wickets for Punjab in the same season and 21 in 2025, when he led their attack to a place in the final.

He also brings a skill set that complements Bumrah. In April, he took 3/22 against Mumbai by swinging the new ball, reversing the old one and bowling a quiet over in the middle. His record at the death is built on yorkers, and a Bumrah-Arshdeep pairing gives Mumbai two specialists for the last four overs.

The deal also resets the captaincy. Rohit Sharma is expected to regain the role, which ends a tenure that produced more defeats than wins.

MORE: Livingstone reacts after R Ashwin's co-host compares him to 'trash'

Punjab finished fifth in 2026 with seven wins from 14 matches and were among the last teams to be eliminated, so the gap to the top four was small. A fast-bowling all-rounder is the rarest profile in T20 cricket, and Hardik was the first player in that category to score 1,000 runs and take 100 wickets in T20Is.

The fit is also clean off the field. Hardik joins purely as a player, with Iyer staying in charge, and the decision to trade for him came from the captain and the coach.

The risks are real, however. Hardik has suffered multiple injury breakdowns and has not played since the last IPL, and Punjab are giving up the bowler who is the franchise's all-time leading wicket-taker.

MORE: Arshdeep Singh-Hardik Pandya swap: Fans react as R Ashwin drops major hint over MI-PBKS trade deal

On paper, Mumbai has addressed a specific issue by bringing in a proven specialist. They needed a second front-line pace option beside Bumrah, and Arshdeep is a better fit for that role than any bowler on their 2026 wicket list. A fresh captain and a fit new-ball partner give a ninth-place side a clear route back into the top four.

Punjab's logic is harder to read. Their second-half bowling was a major issue last season, and they have traded away their best bowler to fix it. That only works if Hardik stays fit and bowls meaningful overs, because an all-rounder who misses games cannot make up for the loss of a leading wicket-taker.

A side that reached the 2025 final deserves the benefit of the doubt, but the deal puts all of the risk on Hardik's body.

The trade will be judged on two numbers: how many league games Hardik plays for Punjab and how well Arshdeep and Bumrah share the death overs for Mumbai. Punjab's answer to replacing Arshdeep's overs will be revealed at the Goa auction on December 16.

Wide receiver Jauan Jennings passed on a possible trade back to the 49ers in order to remain with the Vikings, but he won’t be in Minnesota’s lineup against the Bills on Monday night.

The Vikings ruled Jennings out due to a calf injury that kept him out of practice the last two days. Jennings has six catches for 54 yards this season, but his limited role in the offense didn’t cause him to reach for the exit door last month.

With Jennings out, the Vikings could elevate Odell Beckham Jr. from the practice squad to make his first appearance for the team. The Vikings have until Monday afternoon to elevate him for the game.

Running back Demond Claiborne (knee) will also miss the game. Safeties Theo Jackson (quad) and Jay Ward (knee) are listed as questionable.

#2848. Fantasy Football Rankings: Hayden Winks' WR Blueprint for Week 9

The Blueprint is my weekly column and basically everything that I use to build out the most accurate rankings I can. There will be an RB column, this WR column and a combination column on the onesie positions. You will find film notes and endless charts. Maybe enough charts to stress test the Yahoo website. I kid.

It's impossible to get every ranking thoroughly early in the week, so be sure to keep checking in on these columns through Sunday morning. As always, my full rankings at every position are available.

1. Puka Nacua (at WAS) - 92.5 proj. receiving yards

The Rams offense has really changed recently. In two games without Davante Adams, Nacua's average depth of target is just 3.4 yards downfield. Everything is shallow. It's fine in fantasy because he will rack up catches with ease, and he can power through tackles for first downs. But it does make it a bit harder for the offense to be a threat for 35+ points like they were in previous versions. Nacua is the WR3 on WR1 usage and has a 34% target share since returning to the lineup in Week 4. He's up to 41% targets (!!!) without Adams.

The Commanders have allowed the seventh-most passing yards per game with one of the most underwhelming CB rooms. They'll muck things up in a Diet Coke version of the Brian Flores defense, but that fits with the Rams' quick-hitting approach on offense right now. Los Angeles enters as 5.5-point road favorites with a 26.5-point team total (eighth).

2. Jaxon Smith-Njigba (vs. ARI) - 94.5 proj. receiving yards

JSN has 19.3 half PPR points or more in all but one game, as the clear-cut WR1 overall in fantasy. He's had big games with Drew Lock before, including in Week 2 against these Cardinals, when he had 38.0 half PPR points on 155 yards and three scores.

3. CeeDee Lamb (at IND) - 83.5 proj. receiving yards

Lamb is the WR3 on WR4 usage this season, and the Colts are giving up on defense. Dallas heads into the matchup as 6-point road favorites with a 28.75-point team total (2nd).

4. Ja'Marr Chase (at ATL) - 76.5 proj. receiving yards

Chase is the WR4 on WR9 usage if we remove his Week 4 injury game. Nothing has changed with this offense, aside from now having one of the best RTs in the NFL, Amarius Mims.

5. Tee Higgins (at ATL) - 77.5 proj. receiving yards

Higgins is the WR4 on WR13 usage this season. He's been the WR1, WR2, WR71, WR7, WR8, WR19 and WR39 this season. The Bengals abandoned their under-center pass game officially and will let Joe Burrow cook as he's done since LSU.

6. Drake London (vs. CIN) - 78.5 proj. receiving yards

#2847. ‘We Squashed It’: Hamilton Denies Demands as Leclerc Calls Ferrari Saga Closed

Lewis Hamilton says there were no demands from either side in his talks with Charles Leclerc, as both Ferrari drivers try to move on from their Mexico clash.

The Ferrari saga should now come to an end after the latest comments from Hamilton and Leclerc, following their meeting on Thursday. Team boss Frederic Vasseur reminded both that the F1 team should always come first at all costs.

There are still no set rules of engagement, as he feels it is self-explanatory that the two teammates have to be careful if they are on track together. In the meantime, Italian media reported demands from Hamilton's side.

The reports said Hamilton wanted preference for the rest of the 2026 F1 season since he is ahead of Leclerc in the championship. But the Brit denied any such demand, saying he and Leclerc had talked it through.

"Me and Charles sat and spoke, and we squashed it, and we're moving on," Hamilton told Sky Sports F1. "We still have a huge amount of respect for each other, and I'm glad we had a chat, and now we move on.

"We've been getting along just fine as normal. Sometimes, in those scenarios, it takes having a conversation, and there's been no demands from either side; it's both just giving our points and areas we can do better and support each other. I'm hoping to have better races moving forward."

Lewis Hamilton in qualifying at Interlagos. Image Credit: Scuderia Ferrari

Ferrari teammate Leclerc, meanwhile, took some time away for the birth of his daughter. He arrived in Brazil late and went straight into the meeting. For him, it is a closed chapter after good discussions with Hamilton and even Vasseur.

"I mean, from my perspective, I was very straightforward, of course, and I think it was good to speak," Leclerc told the media. "I think this is always needed after a moment like this. It took proportions that are way too big, and it has been around also for way too long.

"At the same time, it was a very special week for me, so I couldn't really have those discussions before. And it was important to have those discussions, but now I consider that a closed chapter, and I think it will be important to look ahead."

A Ferrari in the wet at Interlagos. Image Credit: Scuderia Ferrari

Leclerc feels it is okay to disagree, but better to speak your mind, as they did. "I really believe that when we speak, things are much better straight away," he said.

"Of course, there is tension; of course, we want to finish ahead of each other, and sometimes we are not going to do things right. And it's okay sometimes to disagree on the way you see things, but at the same time, discussing about those things helps a whole lot.

"I mean, history speaks for itself, and maybe, yeah, looking back, it's maybe something needed. At the same time as I said, sometimes you disagree, and you've got to find common ground."

Asked about Hamilton saying that Leclerc races harder against him than anyone else, the Monegasque didn't want to add fuel. "I wouldn't want to comment on that," he said. "Honestly, there have been way too many comments, and again way too much fuss about it for way too long, so I don't really want to get into those kinds of comments."

#2846. Lakers vs. Pistons Preview: Strength vs. strength

The Lakers (8-2) embark on their first true road trip of the season on Sunday, starting with a stop in Detroit to take on the Pistons (6-2). This is the first contest of a four consecutive games away from home.

Who: Los Angeles Lakers at Detroit Pistons

After a home-heavy start to the season, the Lakers will hit the road for their first road trip of the season, starting with the stiffest test of the slate.

The red-hot start from the Lakers and Luka Dončić offensively has them ranked as the top offense in the league. The Pistons, meanwhile, enter the contest with the best defense in the league, pitting strength vs. strength.

Like Portland, Detroit plays a physical defensive style to try to overwhelm opponents. Offensively, that hasn't deterred the Lakers in either matchup against the Blazers, but Detroit is arguably the best in the league at that style of play, so it'll be a tough test for the purple and gold.

Like the Lakers, the Pistons excel at steals and blocks on the defensive end. However, they are simply average at rebounding, unlike the Lakers, which allows them to close out possessions and bolster their defensive rating.

Detroit allows the third-fewest wide-open 3-point attempts and teams have hit the fewest wide open threes against them in the league. That stat will be put to the test against Luka and Austin Reaves, depending on how they opt to scheme against them defensively.

One area the Lakers could find success is getting to the line. The Pistons put opponents on the line often, ranking 24th in the league in opponent free throw attempts. The Lakers are fourth in the league in free throw attempts per game.

After battling one of the Western Conference's top teams on Friday, the Lakers will have another tough test on Sunday afternoon against one of the East's elites.

It'll be an interesting test for the purple and gold, and another chance to see how they respond to top competition.

Detroit has been off since losing to the Sixers on Wednesday, so this will be a well-rested Pistons team.

After playing in Friday's G League opener for the Coachella Valley Lakers, both Cameron Carr and Bronny James are joining the parent team on the road trip

Luka is a new addition to the injury report with back tightness as he's listed as questionable. It's the same injury that led to him missing a game against the Clippers earlier this season.

Jalen Duran (hamstring strain) remains out for the Pistons while Isiah Joe is also out with a right hip contusion.

#2845. Patriots activate Mack Hollins from IR

#2835. Landry Shamet revels in return to place he became Knicks’ playoff folk hero

CLEVELAND — It had been more than five months since the Knicks stepped inside Rocket Arena, where they conquered the East in a resounding sweep of the Cavaliers to clinch their first NBA Finals berth in 26 years.

It was in that Eastern Conference finals that Landry Shamet emerged as a folk hero, beginning with his instantly iconic game-tying 3-pointer that miraculously bounced in during the 22-point fourth quarter comeback in Game 1.

After being ousted from the rotation in the first round, Shamet went 11-for-12 on 3-pointers against the Cavaliers, setting a single-series postseason record.

When Shamet returned to the site of the team's celebration Saturday morning, he was welcomed by some of the best memories of his career.

"It's human nature, you're gonna revert back and think back to the last time you were in the building," Shamet said before scoring nine points in the Knicks' 109-97 win over the Cavaliers on Saturday night. "I had a quick little firing of that walking in for shootaround, but I think the general sense was that was last year. That was great. You can have those memories and hang on to that as long as we want, but ultimately this year is a new year and a new endeavor."

Landry Shamet shoots a jumper during the Knicks game against the Cavaliers on Nov. 7, 2026 in Cleveland. NBAE via Getty Images

Shamet's ninth season in the league is unlike any he's experienced.

After spending his first six years with five teams, Shamet has started his third straight season with the same team for the first time.

After playing on nonguaranteed deals the past two seasons in New York — and claiming the final roster spot last fall — Shamet, 29, is now in the first year of a four-year, $24 million contract that he signed with the Knicks this summer.

Landry Shamet hits a 3-pointer during the Knicks' Game 1 win over the Cavaliers in the Eastern Conference Finals, a game in which he became a folk hero. Jason Szenes for New York Post

"The biggest thing is just being comfortable with the guys on the floor, second year with [head coach] Mike [Brown]," said Shamet who started for the injured Josh Hart in Saturday night's win. "I think that just breeds confidence. Familiarity breeds confidence. There's no denying that. It allows you to get to the point of conversations quicker. It makes for a good formula to find success."

Entering Saturday, Shamet was averaging 9.4 points — ranking fourth on the Knicks — while shooting 42.5 percent on 3-pointers and playing his most minutes (24.9) in seven seasons.

Shamet made his first start of the season — in place of the injured Josh Hart — in Wednesday's blowout win over the Bulls. In the Knicks' previous two wins, Shamet was on the floor for the closing stretch, as the struggling Mikal Bridges remained on the bench.

Shamet does not know when he will be needed. He does not need to, likening his spot on the team to that of his high school friend Aaron Ashby, who just delivered one of the greatest postseason runs by a reliever for the World Series champion Brewers.

"Especially with [my] role, I think I take a lot from my buddy Ashby, bullpen guy, you don't know when you're gonna get thrown in, what the situation's gonna be," Shamet said. "My job might look a little different from night to night. If I'm changing my approach every night, that's not setting myself up for a good situation.

"I think in the past in my career when I was younger I would try to overcomplicate things and think I have to reinvent the wheel. I try to just keep it as simple as possible, reduce it down to my job, my impact and just play my game."

#2834. The 1 trade Eagles must make in final week before 2026 NFL trade deadline

The 1 trade Eagles must make in final week before 2026 NFL trade deadline appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

It's (almost) here, Philadelphia Eagles fans: the 2026 NFL trade deadline.

Soon, fans around the NFL will get to see who ends up playing where, how many stars have to find new homes, and which teams are willing to go all in on 2026, or punt on the campaign in favor of the future.

In the past, for the vast majority of the 21st century, in fact, the Eagles have firmly been buyers, using the shrewd dealings of Howie Roseman to cash out future picks for present contributors.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

If it worked, like with Jay Ajayi, great, the Eagles' ceiling elevated considerably and Roseman paid up with a new, long-term contract. And if it didn't, that's cool too; acquiring Jaelan Phillips didn't really help the Eagles' Super Bowl chances in 2025, but when he left in free agency, he effectively got the team back the pick they surrendered to bring him into the program, even if it comes in 2027 instead of 2026.

In 2026, the Eagles are firmly sellers, with teams around the NFL trying to pry away a few members of the Super Bowl LIX roster in the hopes of getting them to Super Bowl LXI. Some players, like Saquon Barkley, have been publicly removed from the trade block, while others, like Moro Ojomo, have noted that the Eagles want to keep them long-term instead of pulling off a trade, but as the sharks circle and the time ticks down, more deals will arrive that Roseman has to navigate, some of which could change the franchise forever.

With very few players truly untradeable – Jordan Mailata, Quinyon Mitchell, Jalen Hurts, as he deals with blood clots – there is one player who is almost certainly not going to be traded at the deadline, but could garner a massive return from a team like the Jacksonville Jaguars, who are reportedly looking for a defensive tackle desperately: Jalen Carter. While from a talent standpoint, Carter is maybe the Eagles' best defensive player when he's firing on all cylinders, but considering how infrequently that happens, it might be the perfect time to cash out while his value is at an all-time high.

When the Eagles landed Carter in the first round of the 2022 NFL Draft, it looked like the steal of the century.

Using a draft pick originally owned by the New Orleans Saints, which the Eagles artificially improved by allowing the Washington Commanders to beat them in the regular season finale, fans watched in awe as a player widely considered the most talented in the entire class slid down the board, with a minor trade of a fourth-round pick the only requirement to move from nine to eight in order to get a deal done.

From the point where Carter took the field as a rookie, he instantly impressed, turning in snaps, drives, quarters, and even games where he looked like the best player on the field regardless of uniform. Standing 6-foot-3, 314 pounds, Carter's unique combination of bend and power has routinely wrecked interior offensive lines with ease, collapsing pockets and ruining whatever plan a quarterback had at the snap.

The problem: Carter simply doesn't do it often enough.

Now in 2026, Carter has an excuse. The 25-year-old suffered a hairline fracture in his wrist early in the season and, as a result, has been playing with a cast on his hand. And yet, there have been games where Carter caused havoc all the same, recording five tackles, three tackles for a loss, and two sacks against the Jaguars in Week 5 after doing very little in the two games before and after.

This trend of a dominant game followed by unremarkable performance has unfortunately been a trend for Carter as a pro. Unlike, say, Jeffery Simmons, who was traded for a massive package back in October, the Eagles never quite know what they will get from Carter every time he takes the field, and as a result, if he's off, the entire defense tends to be as well. Sure, every player has a down game from time to time, but for the most part, when Zack Baun, Quinyon Mitchell, or even Jalyx Hunt takes the field, Vic Fangio knows what he's going to get, and that just hasn't been the case for Carter.

Could Carter put it all together and become the next Fletcher Cox, or even surpass him, which he has the talent to do? Sure, he could theoretically play another decade and will only get better as he enters Year 5, 6, and beyond. But it's also possible Carter remains a very expensive question mark on a team with a lot of questions surrounding their future.

Eagles: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 third-round pick, 2028 first-round pick, Brian Thomas Jr.

Jaguars: Jalen Carter, 2027 fifth-round pick

Mandatory Credit: Travis Register-Imagn Images

If the Eagles are going to trade Carter – which they probably won't, but should at least consider – the conversation doesn't even start unless at least one first-round pick is on the table.

Sure, some fans will want a second first-round pick or at least an additional Day 2 selection, but at the bare minimum, the Eagles need to add another one, especially in 2028, when they will have three at their disposal, and Hurts could theoretically no longer be on the team. But what if they could also add a depreciated asset who has produced at the NFL level but is currently struggling to consistently reach the top end of his ceiling?

Fortunately, the Jaguars have that on their roster too in Brian Thomas Jr., who looked like a legit WR1 as a rookie before becoming an afterthought in Liam Coen's scheme.

Initially drafted in the first round of the 2024 NFL Draft out of LSU, Thomas was one of the more controversial players in his class, a deep threat who ran a limited scheme in college, but quickly proved doubters wrong right out of the gate, where he recorded 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns on his way to a Pro Bowl appearance. He recorded an average of 75.4 yards per game, including 14.7 per reception, and looked like the kind of player who could pair up with Trevor Lawrence for years to come.

And yet, in 2026, Thomas' yards per game are under 20, and he has recorded zero yards in three of the eight games he's appeared in.

With the rest of this year, all of next year, and a fifth-year option still on the table for the 2028 NFL season, BTJ presents a unique reclamation project who could help stretch the field for Joe Milton now and potentially develop an expanded role in Philadelphia long-term if he recaptures his early success.

Moving on from Carter also opens the door for Ojomo actually getting that extension he mentioned, forming a one-two punch with Jordan Davis that costs as much as the "Baby Rhino" on his own. With Hunt, Mitchell, DeJean, Nolan Smith, and Jeremiah Trotter Jr. all in need of new contracts in the not-too-distant future, the Eagles could effectively spread Carter's money out over multiple players and use the capital he garners to add even more young, cost-controlled talent who can fill foundational roles for years to come.

Would the Eagles be better off without Carter in 2026, 2027, or even 2028? Most likely not, but with the decisions to trade away Brown and Jurgens already looking like genius moves, who knows? Maybe Roseman can take advantage of the Jaguars' desperation and pull off another monster trade. Considering how much James Gladstone gave up for Travis Hunter, it's not like Jacksonville is particularly stingy when they identify a player they like, so why not take advantage of that and set the Eagles up for their next generation of Super Bowl contenders?

#2830. Warriors forward Georges Niang gets a tech after shove war with Magic

SAN FRANCISCO ― Golden State Warriors forward Georges Niang has brought added toughness to the team, and it rears its head often throughout the game.

Niang and Orlando Magic center Wendell Carter Jr. were separated by teammates before being assessed technical fouls a brief push-off and animated words between the two during a regular-season meeting between the Warriors and Magic on Saturday, Nov. 7 at Chase Center in San Francisco.

With 9 minutes and 17 seconds in the second quarter, Carter received an entry pass inside the paint, and Niang, out of position, committed an intentional foul, wrapping up Carter before he could get off the ground.

Warriors forward Draymond Green and guard Gary Payton II de-escalated the situation, protecting Niang.

After officials reviewed the play, double-technical fouls were handed out to Niang and Carter.

Niang has mixed it up with anyone and everyone showing that he's a guy that's willing to scrap, claw and get in opponents face. He won't allow others to impose their will on his team. And when the Warriors want to get physical, Niang is down for the get down.

The type of energy, that type of spunk is what fellow teammate Green raves about. Green has already had to hold Niang back when getting into it with Miami Heat forward Bobby Portis and Los Angeles Lakers guard Collin Sexton.

Niang wasn't on the court during the dust up with Phoenix Suns and guard Dillon Brooks, but he looked on as if he wanted to get in the mix.

"I love that, I love that type of energy, by the way," Green said. "George has been incredible for us and the way he shoots the basketball. Crazy thing is he hasn't even shot it at a level that he shoots the ball at and yet the impact that he's had on this team on every aspect of the game. He's so smart."

Niang is avergaing 7.9 points, 3.1 rebounds, and 1.7 assists per game for the Warriors through nine games. He's a career 39.7% 3-point shooter but has only connected on 30.6% of attempts so far in the 2026-27 season.

Still, it's the little things that Niang does that makes him valuable to the Warriors roster.

"What an addition," Green said. "That's one of those signings that people look at like 'aw man' but then you look up and this guy, you can't keep him off the floor. He's been absolutely great for us. I have absolutely loved being his teammate."

"I'll be honest, I have times (when) I do some random (expletive) out there, especially on the defensive end. But even on offense, and he just picks up on it like that. ... Really fun player to play with."

No. 1 Miami lost. No. 6 Kentucky was embarrassed. Another Top 10 team, BYU, went down. And Ohio State, a program that occupied the No. 2 ranking just a week earlier, suffered another defeat.

Meanwhile, Georgia, which itself experienced the humiliation of losing as the nation's No. 1 team earlier this season, suddenly looks like the team to beat again.

According to The Upset Report, 21 teams ranked in the AP Top 10 have lost during the first 10 weeks of the season. Seven losses have come against teams occupying the No. 1 or No. 2 positions.

Seven times, one of the two highest-ranked teams in America has walked off the field defeated.

Miami entered Saturday sitting atop the first College Football Playoff rankings, undefeated and positioned as the leading contender for the national championship.

The Hurricanes left Notre Dame Stadium with a 31-24 loss and an entirely different outlook.

Notre Dame quarterback CJ Carr threw for 319 yards and three touchdowns, helping the 11th-ranked Fighting Irish deliver the weekend's biggest result.

The loss doesn't necessarily eliminate Miami from championship contention. That's one of the advantages of the expanded playoff format.

A team that appeared to control its destiny must now confront the same questions that have followed nearly every other national contender this season.

Was Miami overrated? Was Notre Dame underrated? Or is the difference between the nation's best teams simply smaller than anyone wants to admit?

The Hurricanes aren't alone in trying to answer those questions.

The Bulldogs looked every bit like a national championship contender Saturday, dismantling No. 10 Ole Miss 42-7 in one of the most impressive performances of the season.

Georgia led 28-0 at halftime and thoroughly overwhelmed an opponent that entered the weekend with legitimate playoff aspirations.

If you watched only that game, you might conclude that Georgia is clearly the best team in America.

Georgia was the nation's top-ranked team when unranked Auburn pulled off a stunning 27-24 upset in Week 7.

The Tigers entered that game as 19.5-point underdogs.

Now Georgia is positioned to return to No. 1 following Miami's defeat.

A team can look unbeatable one week, completely vulnerable the next, and then emerge as the national championship favorite all over again.

Georgia may very well win the whole thing.

But would anyone really be surprised if the Bulldogs suffered another stunning defeat before the season ends?

The season's growing list of casualties is remarkable.

Through Week 10, The Upset Report has documented:

Seven losses by teams ranked No. 1 or No. 2

Those numbers help explain why the national championship picture remains so unsettled.

And the individual upsets are even more revealing.

In Week 2, Oklahoma State stunned No. 6 Oregon 39-31 despite entering as a 24.5-point underdog.

In Week 6, unranked Oklahoma knocked off No. 1 Texas 27-24.

A week later, Auburn defeated top-ranked Georgia.

Then came UCF's 39-31 victory over No. 2 BYU in Week 8.

And in Week 9, unranked USC handed No. 2 Ohio State a 30-18 defeat.

Saturday added Miami's loss to Notre Dame and Tennessee's 34-6 demolition of sixth-ranked Kentucky.

It is difficult to build a convincing argument for any team being untouchable when so many supposed national championship favorites have already been beaten.

For perspective, the legendary 2007 season remains one of college football's most chaotic years. The Upset Report's historical comparison shows that 2007 had produced more losses by ranked teams through Week 10 than 2026.

So declaring this season the most unpredictable in history would be premature.

But there is no denying that 2026 belongs in the conversation about seasons that have repeatedly overturned the established national hierarchy.

Perhaps no recent example illustrates the volatility better than Ohio State.

The Buckeyes were ranked No. 2 entering their October 31 matchup with USC.

A week later, Ohio State fell again, this time 41-28 against Oregon.

The Ducks, who themselves suffered one of the season's most shocking losses against Oklahoma State in September, erased a 14-point deficit and scored 38 unanswered points against the Buckeyes.

Oregon was once the victim of a stunning upset. Now the Ducks have delivered one of the biggest results of November.

Ohio State went from national championship favorite to a team facing serious questions about its playoff prospects in barely more than a week.

Kentucky experienced its own dramatic reversal Saturday.

The Wildcats entered their matchup with Tennessee ranked sixth in the initial CFP rankings, having emerged as one of the season's biggest surprises.

They left Knoxville following a 34-6 defeat.

Tennessee held Kentucky scoreless in the second half and dominated the fourth quarter.

And the Volunteers, who had already defeated Alabama earlier this season, suddenly have another signature victory that could dramatically improve their playoff position.

The lesson is becoming impossible to ignore.

A team's résumé can change dramatically in three hours.

Utah and UCLA emerged from Saturday still undefeated.

The third-ranked Utes defeated No. 9 BYU 28-20 in the Holy War, while eighth-ranked UCLA improved to 9-0 with a 34-20 victory over Minnesota.

Those programs deserve enormous credit for navigating a season that has swallowed so many contenders.

But their unbeaten records don't guarantee anything.

Utah had to survive a difficult rivalry matchup against BYU. UCLA faced another competitive test before pulling away from Minnesota.

Both teams have demonstrated that they know how to win.

Neither has demonstrated that losing is impossible.

And that's what makes this season so fascinating.

Even the programs that have avoided the chaos have spent months watching it consume nearly everyone around them.

The 12-team College Football Playoff has introduced an intriguing wrinkle into a season defined by upsets.

In the old four-team format, one unexpected defeat could destroy a championship dream.

Now, a team can absorb a loss, regroup and remain very much alive.

That makes the playoff race more forgiving, but it also creates the possibility of an extraordinarily unpredictable postseason.

Consider what the bracket might look like if teams such as Georgia, Miami, Alabama, Texas, Tennessee, Notre Dame, Oregon and Ohio State all remain in contention.

Others have lost to teams they were heavily favored to defeat.

Several have alternated between dominant performances and inexplicable disappointments.

The selection committee must somehow sort through those contradictions.

And then, once the bracket is established, the teams must actually play the games.

If the regular season has taught us anything, it's that rankings and reputations offer remarkably little protection once the ball is kicked off.

Georgia has a compelling argument following its destruction of Ole Miss.

Utah can point to an undefeated record and another impressive victory over a ranked opponent.

Alabama has recovered from earlier setbacks and delivered a convincing 31-13 victory over LSU.

Texas has survived a difficult schedule and strengthened its position with Saturday's 34-20 win at Missouri.

Notre Dame just beat the nation's No. 1 team.

Tennessee has victories over Alabama and Kentucky.

Every one of those teams can make a case for belonging in the championship discussion.

Every one also faces questions, whether about past defeats, remaining opponents, schedule strength or the ability to sustain its current form.

That uncertainty is the defining characteristic of the 2026 season.

There may be teams with better résumés, superior talent or more favorable paths to the postseason.

And that is precisely what makes the next several weeks so compelling.

The first College Football Playoff rankings were released Tuesday.

Four days later, the No. 1 team had lost, the No. 6 team had been blown out, another Top 10 contender had fallen, and the entire championship conversation had shifted.

There are still regular-season games to play, conference championships to settle and playoff invitations to distribute.

The championship won't be decided until January 25 in Las Vegas.

Between now and then, how many more favorites will fall?

How many fan bases will spend a Saturday night convinced their championship dreams are finished, only to discover a week later that they're right back in the conversation?

How many teams will look unbeatable before suddenly looking ordinary?

That's the beauty of this extraordinary college football season.

For the fans of every championship contender, there is reason to dream.

But after everything we've witnessed through 10 weeks, there is absolutely no reason to feel safe.

The 2026 national championship is still there for the taking. And nobody should be surprised by who takes it.

#2824. 2. Bundesliga: Dresden off the bottom with convincing victory over Fürth

First half goals from Robert Wagner and Ben Bobzien had the hosts firmly in control at the half. Vincent Vermeij added a second-half strike to make it 3-0 before Hendry Blank saw red for the visitors capping off a miserable evening for Fürth. Dresden made a lively start at the Rudolf-Harbig-Stadion, although Greuther Fürth initially looked dangerous going forward. The visitors came close to opening the scoring through Omar Sillah, whose effort drifted narrowly wide after a defensive mix-up, before Sacha Bansé tested Lennart Grill with a powerful effort from distance. Dynamo also threatened at the other end, with Patrice Čović missing a promising opportunity from inside the penalty area.

However, it was the hosts who eventually broke the deadlock in the 31st minute. Niklas Hauptmann did well to turn away from two opponents before laying the ball into the path of Robert Wagner, whose first-time effort took a deflection off Hendry Blank and wrong-footed goalkeeper Florian Hellstern.

Dynamo doubled their advantage ten minutes later, with Ben Bobzien finding the net in similarly fortunate circumstances. After receiving the ball from Tobias Raschl, the forward cut inside before seeing his effort deflected by Blank and loop into the top corner, leaving Hellstern with little chance of making a save.

Fürth almost reduced the deficit before the interval, with Sillah narrowly missing a cross from Gian-Luca Itter before the latter saw two efforts blocked and deflected wide. Despite those opportunities, Thomas Stamm's side headed into the break with a deserved two-goal advantage.

The hosts continued to apply pressure after the restart and effectively put the contest beyond doubt in the 55th minute. Bobzien turned provider this time, setting up Vincent Vermeij, who had the simple task of rolling the ball into an unguarded net to make it 3-0.

Fürth's evening then went from bad to worse seven minutes later when Blank received his marching orders. Having already been booked in the opening minute, the defender brought down Bobzien as he threatened to break through on goal, receiving a second yellow card and leaving the visitors with ten men for the remainder of the contest.

Dresden looked increasingly comfortable against their numerical disadvantage, with Čović coming close to adding a fourth in the 73rd minute, only for his effort to be blocked by Krisztián Keresztes close to the goal line.

The hosts ultimately saw out a convincing 3-0 victory, recording another impressive home result following their recent wins over Magdeburg and in the cup against Schalke. The three points also provide a significant boost to Dresden's hopes of climbing away from the bottom of the 2. Bundesliga table, while Fürth will be disappointed with an evening in which defensive misfortune and Blank's dismissal contributed to a heavy defeat.
